sections.heading: Employment Termination Under Bangladesh Labour Act 2006
sections.content: The relationship between employers and workers in Bangladesh is heavily regulated by the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006. Under the current law, an employer cannot simply fire a worker without following specific legal procedures. The law categorizes the end of employment into several types: discharge (for physical/mental incapacity), dismissal (for severe misconduct), retrenchment (due to redundancy), and termination (general ending of employment). Each category has specific notice periods, procedural requirements, and compensation structures that employers are legally obligated to fulfill to avoid claims of wrongful termination. sections.heading: Notice Periods and Procedural Fairness
sections.content: Procedural fairness is central to Bangladesh labour law. For a general termination of a permanent worker, the employer must provide a written notice of 120 days for monthly rated workers, or 60 days for other workers. Alternatively, the employer can pay wages for the notice period in lieu of the notice. In cases of dismissal for misconduct (like theft, insubordination), a strict domestic inquiry procedure must be followed, including issuing a show-cause notice and allowing the worker to defend themselves, before any final decision is made. sections.heading: Compensation and Gratuity Calculation
sections.content: When a permanent worker is terminated without misconduct, they are entitled to significant compensation. A terminated worker is legally entitled to 30 days of wages for every completed year of service, or gratuity, whichever is higher. Gratuity calculation is crucial: it is generally calculated at 30 days basic wage for every completed year if service is more than 6 months but less than 10 years, and 45 days basic wage per year if continuous service exceeds 10 years. sections.heading: Special Protections for Female Workers
sections.content: The Labour Act provides stringent protections for female workers, particularly regarding maternity. It is illegal to issue a notice of dismissal, discharge, or termination to a woman within a certain period before or after her maternity leave if the notice expires during that period. Any attempt to terminate a pregnant worker to avoid paying maternity benefits is considered wrongful and renders the termination void. sections.heading: Filing a Complaint in the Labour Court
sections.content: If a worker faces wrongful termination or is denied legal dues, they must first send a grievance notice to the employer in writing within 30 days of the incident. The employer has 30 days to respond. If the employer rejects the grievance or fails to respond, the worker can file a formal case in the Labour Court within the next 30 days. The Labour Court specializes in employment disputes and has the authority to examine the fairness of the termination, order the payment of due compensation, or even order reinstatement of the worker. sections.heading: Reinstatement vs. Compensation
sections.content: When the Labour Court finds a termination to be illegal or unjustified, it has two primary remedies. It can order the employer to reinstate the worker to their previous position with full back pay, treating the dismissal as if it never happened. Alternatively, if the court deems reinstatement impractical due to a ruined working relationship, it can order the employer to pay enhanced compensation in addition to the statutory dues. faqs.question: Can an employer fire me immediately for theft?
faqs.answer: They can suspend you immediately, but they cannot formally dismiss you without issuing a show-cause notice and holding an internal inquiry to prove the misconduct.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a case in the Labour Court?
faqs.answer: You must act quickly. First, send a grievance notice within 30 days of termination. If unresolved, you generally have 30 days from the employers decision to file in court.

faqs.question: What is the difference between termination and retrenchment?
faqs.answer: Termination is a general end of employment, while retrenchment specifically means laying off workers due to redundancy or downsizing of the business.

faqs.question: Are all employees covered by the Labour Act?
faqs.answer: Most industrial and commercial workers are covered. However, certain managerial or administrative staff may fall outside the definition of a "worker" and are governed by their contract.
